newsitem.title: UK: NYMEX-IPE link to boost oil dealing, squeeze SIMEX.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX-IPE link to boost oil dealing, squeeze SIMEX.

text.p: Plans to cut the cost of oil futures trading are likely to help over-the-counter derivatives markets as well as giving a much needed boost to exchange-based contracts, oil dealers said on Tuesday.

The New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) said on Tuesday it was in talks with London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) about a joint electronic trading system and other links aimed at trimming costs.
But closer ties between the two largest oil exchanges were bound to intensify pressure on the smaller Singapore Monetary Exchange (SIMEX), dealers said.

NYMEX president Patrick Thompson said the exchanges were not contemplating a full-blown merger but were mulling joining contracts through electronic trading systems and cross-margining -- reducing the amount of cash traders have to pay up front for spread trades between the exchanges' contracts.
Besides benefitting the exchanges' members, Thompson said the talks were also spurred by concern that after years of rapid growth, volumes in crude and oil product futures had been trailing off.
Any boost in exchange traded volumes due to lower trading costs is also likely to help the telephone-based derivatives or swaps markets which have also suffered in recent years.
"More liquidity on the floor is bound to help swaps," said Micheal Levy of brokers GFI Group Inc in London.
The average monthly volume traded on the NYMEX crude contract averaged 1.91 million contracts last year after peaking at over two million per month in 1993 and 1994.
By comparison the 1980s saw huge growth with volumes jumping to 1.98 million in 1990 from 690,000 in 1986.
The IPE Brent crude contract grew rapidly during the 1990s but has also flattened out since 1994.

Swaps, which are tied directly to the IPE's Brent and gas oil contracts, are widely traded in Europe. Crack spread swaps between gas oil and Brent futures are used by oil refiners to hedge profit margins.

They are traded over the telephone but are priced against the floor-traded futures contracts. When oil refiners want to adjust their positions, they often do so by trading the underlying futures contract.
"Particularly on the gas oil cracks were see a lot of potential synergy," said GFI's Levy.

While the big Western oil exchanges appear to be cosying up to each other, the smaller Singapore Monetary Exchange (SIMEX), which trades Brent futures during the Asian day, risks being sidelined, dealers said.
Any new deal between NYMEX and the IPE would "call into question the IPE's link with SIMEX" said Nigel Saperia, managing director of the oil trading division at Bankers Trust International in London.
IPE officials have already said they want to reclaim half an hour of Brent futures trading at the start of the London day from SIMEX.
Thompson said discussions on posting the IPE Brent contract on NYMEX's out-of-hours ACCESS system were "at the working-group stage".
